“BAN TRUMP FROM CANADA FOREVER?” — Cross-Border Petitions Spark Heated Debate Over Border Inadmissibility.

A wave of online campaigns and formal petitions submitted to the House of Commons of Canada have called on the federal government to bar Donald Trump and associated political figures from entering the country:

Proponents of an entry ban cite Canada's strict Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), under which foreign nationals convicted of indictable criminal offenses abroad are routinely deemed inadmissible at the border. Petitioners also point to ongoing cross-border tariff disputes and political rhetoric.

Canadian political leaders, including Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, have dismissed calls to block U.S. leaders, underscoring that diplomatic engagement, international summits, and maintaining open transit across the world's longest shared border are vital to Canada’s national and economic security.

Critics argue that weaponizing border control against mainstream American political movements sets a dangerous precedent, alienates Canada’s closest trading partner, and risks severe diplomatic retaliation.

Should Canada enforce strict criminal inadmissibility laws regardless of political status, or is calling to ban major American political figures an unrealistic and damaging overreach? Cast your vote in the comments below.

"We will not apologize."

Pete Hegseth just took the podium at the Pentagon and drew a hard line in the sand: zero excuses, zero backing down when it comes to the border and the cartels poisoning American streets.

The administration is framing this as an aggressive, long-overdue offensive to shut down trafficking corridors once and for all.

Critics and policy veterans are pushing back, arguing that military posturing at a podium doesn't fix broken cross-border intelligence or solve the crisis at ground level.

Meanwhile, communities burying victims of synthetic opioids are demanding immediate, visible results—not just more political rhetoric.

Here’s the real question: Does a hard-line, military-first stance actually crush the cartels, or does it just create a diplomatic nightmare while the drugs keep flowing?

Enforcement teams on the ground are already facing ruthless, evolving syndicates that adapt the second pressure ramps up.

Allies across the border are pushing back on unilateral talk, raising the stakes for regional stability.

Are you backing Hegseth’s no-apology stance, or is this just theater?

ormer FBI Co-Deputy Director Dan Bongino just dropped a three-line warning on X as the nationwide FAA ground stop unfolds.

"Panic kills. Be careful. Stay safe."

With radio and communications outages hitting major air traffic centers and the FBI now probing whether a software update triggered the disruption, Bongino's brief message is raising serious questions.

Should we be preparing for the worst, or is he simply urging people to stay calm while officials sort out the facts? Drop your thoughts below.

#DanBongino #FAA

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin just stepped out at the White House to confirm all flights are accounted for during the FAA's nationwide ground stop.

Mullin said there is "no indication as of yet this was a nefarious attack against us," adding that aircraft already in the air are being handled "case by case." Reports indicate radio frequency outages hit air traffic control centers covering Chicago, New York, and Boston before spreading nationwide — marking only the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11, after the January 2023 outage.

Are you seeing flight delays or cancellations in your city right now? Drop an update in the comments.

#FAA #GroundStop #HomelandSecurity

The Federal Aviation Administration just issued a sweeping nationwide ground stop halting departures across U.S. airports — marking only the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11, following the January 2023 outage.

The FAA cited "extraordinary circumstances," safety concerns, and a communication issue behind the sudden halt, leaving travelers and aviation watchers waiting on more details from federal officials.

Are you or someone you know stuck at an airport right now? Drop your airport and what you're seeing in the comments.

#FAA #GroundStop #Aviation #BreakingNews #AirTrafficControl #TravelAlert #SRSClips

U.S. Reconnaissance Marines with the III Marine Expeditionary Force have teamed up with the Korea Coast Guard (ROKCG) in South Korea to conduct comprehensive Visit, Board, Search, and Seizure (VBSS) training drills, sharply refining combined maritime interdiction capabilities across the Pacific theater.

Moving through complex shipboard mockups, stairwells, and watertight hatchways, combined assault teams drilled dynamic room-clearing, stair transitions, and tactile vessel control under simulated combat conditions to counter maritime contraband and hostile boarding scenarios.

Alongside tactical close-quarters battle (CQB) clearance, the bilateral training cycle combined close-in defensive tactics, combatives/jiu-jitsu techniques, and tactical live-fire ranges to align operational standard operating procedures between forward-deployed Marines and Korean maritime law enforcement operators.

 Executed under bilateral defense cooperation frameworks, these high-readiness interdiction drills ensure allied forces maintain seamless, rapid interoperability to protect contested maritime choke points, enforce maritime law, and preserve freedom of navigation across the region.

Marine Lance Cpl. Jabari N. Thompson
Died July 17, 2011 Serving During Operation Enduring Freedom

President Trump's Executive Order 14341 on burning the American flag continues to spark fierce debate across the country.

Signed in August 2025, the order directs the Department of Justice to prosecute flag-burning incidents under existing criminal and fire-safety laws, while Trump remarked at the signing that offenders should get "one year in jail." Meanwhile, First Amendment advocates point to the Supreme Court's 1989 Texas v. Johnson ruling protecting peaceful flag burning as symbolic speech.

Should burning the American flag be a crime punishable by prison, or protected under the First Amendment? Drop your take below.

#AmericanFlag #FirstAmendment #FreeSpeech

Resurfaced remarks from California First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom are making the rounds again after she called President Donald Trump a "con artist, a predator, a malignant narcissist in chief, and the worst president in our nation's history" at a November 2025 rally.

With Gov. Gavin Newsom and Trump's supporters trading shots heading into the next national cycle, do remarks like this fire up the base or push undecided voters away?

Drop your reaction in the comments.

ELON MUSK PROPOSES APP FOR STRANGERS TO POST BILLS & BORED BILLIONAIRES TO PAY THEM: WOULD YOU UPLOAD YOUR DEBT?

In a viral post on X, Elon Musk floated a provocative concept that immediately ignited a global debate across social platforms:

"Making an app where you upload your bills and bored billionaires swipe right to pay them"

The Tinder-style debt-relief concept envisions a platform where everyday people upload past-due utility bills, medical invoices, auto loans, or grocery receipts, giving ultra-wealthy individuals a direct, gamified swipe-to-pay interface to wipe out balances on the spot.

A viral post making the rounds claims a U.S. soldier was mocked for praying before missions — only for her commander to ask her to return because her prayers were working.

Whether you served downrange or supported someone who did, faith in uniform means a lot to a lot of service members. Should prayer before missions always be welcomed in a unit?

Drop your thoughts in the comments.

The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery has been guarded every single minute of every single day since July 2, 1937.

Through pouring rain, snowstorms, hurricanes, and the dead of night, sentinels from the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment — The Old Guard — march 21 steps along a 63-foot mat and pause for 21 seconds, honoring the 21-gun salute. And if a visitor forgets where they are and starts talking or laughing, those guards will shut it down on the spot.

Have you ever visited the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in person? Drop your experience below.

#TombOfTheUnknownSoldier #TheOldGuard

“PARATROOPERS DON’T CLOCK OUT: HEARD GUNSHOTS & RAN DOWNSTAIRS WITH IMPROVISED MEDICAL GEAR.”

Paratroopers don't clock out. When gunfire erupted outside his apartment building, Sergeant Brian Lieberman didn't lock his door and wait for the police. He ran straight into the courtyard, found a victim with an open chest wound, and built an airtight chest seal with plastic wrap and tape to keep her lungs from collapsing.

On June 5, 2023, then-Specialist Brian R. Lieberman—a combat medic with the 1st Brigade Combat Team, 82nd Airborne Division—was off-duty at his apartment complex in Fayetteville, North Carolina, when rapid gunfire shattered the evening quiet.

Without body armor or advanced medical equipment, he grabbed his legally owned firearm and sprinted downstairs toward the active shooter:

Sprinting to the Fire: Arriving in the courtyard, Lieberman identified himself as an Army combat medic and located a female victim suffering from a critical penetrating sucking chest wound.

Shielding Under Secondary Fire: As he began treating her, the active shooter circled back in a vehicle and opened fire directly at them. Lieberman threw his body across the wounded woman to act as a human shield, drew his sidearm, returned fire, and drove the shooter away.

The Improvised Chest Seal: With air and blood entering her chest cavity and no standard trauma kit on hand, Lieberman improvised an occlusive chest seal using a plastic bag and tape, venting trapped air to prevent a fatal tension pneumothorax.

Fighting Traumatic Shock: He treated the victim for hypovolemic shock and kept her conscious until Fayetteville Police and EMS arrived, saving her life.

For his valor and composure, Colonel Jason Schuerger presented Sergeant Lieberman with the Soldier's Medal—the U.S. Army's highest non-combat award for heroism. In October 2026, he was formally recognized as an Angel of the Battlefield recipient.

“Without a doubt our Airborne medics move to the sound of gunfire to save lives,” said Col. Schuerger. “Of course he moved to the sound of gunfire, of course he administered aid, of course he saved somebody's life.”

Lieberman’s guidance to fellow medics reflects the heart of the Airborne:

“I always tell my junior medics to never lose their passion for the craft of medicine. That way no matter where they are, no matter what they're doing, they can always be there for someone on their worst day.”

All American valor in action.

In April 1967, then-Second Lieutenant James Capers Jr. led a nine-man Force Recon team near Phu Loc, Vietnam, when they were ambushed by a much larger enemy force.

Hit by gunfire, shrapnel, and a broken leg, Capers kept directing supporting fires and refused to board the rescue helicopter until every single Marine on his team was safely extracted.

Fifty-nine years later, at 88 years old, he stood in the White House and became the first Black Marine officer awarded the Medal of Honor.

Drop a Semper Fi below for Major James Capers Jr.

He fell down a mountain… and somehow they still found him.

Most people assume when a 9-year-old dog disappears into the woods and goes silent for days, the ending isn’t good.
This one was different.
Archie, a yellow Lab, took a hard fall on Poor Mountain in Roanoke County and got stuck far down the slope. His family heard him howling from the mountainside and searched for two full days with neighbors and volunteers.
On Wednesday, firefighters from Roanoke County Fire & Rescue climbed down with ropes, found him, and carried him back up in a litter — tired, a little banged up, but very much alive.
He’s home now. Warm. Safe. Back by the fire.
Sometimes the ones we think are gone for good are just waiting for someone stubborn enough to come get them.

"Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave."
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed just fired off a direct public challenge to Donald Trump on X, putting universal healthcare right back at the center of the political firestorm.  
Bullet The Pitch: El-Sayed is calling on Trump to break from traditional party lines and deliver guaranteed, cradle-to-grave healthcare coverage for every single U.S. citizen.  
Bullet The Backlash: Fiscal conservatives and free-market critics are immediately pushing back, warning that government-run healthcare guarantees come with massive tax hikes, ballooning national debt, and rationed care.
Bullet The Reality: With millions of working-class families crushed by skyrocketing premiums and medical bills, the healthcare fight isn't going anywhere—and both sides are trying to claim they have the real fix.
Here’s the real question: Would guaranteed healthcare from cradle to grave actually save American families, or would it bankrupt the country and destroy quality of care?
Bullet Supporters argue that the richest nation on earth shouldn't leave citizens choosing between bankruptcy and seeing a doctor.
Bullet Opponents insist that government-mandated care leads to endless waitlists, bloated bureaucracy, and worse outcomes.
Where do you stand on El-Sayed’s challenge to Trump?

“HE BOMBED A SCHOOL FULL OF LITTLE GIRLS. PETE HEGSETH IS A WAR CRIMINAL.”

A viral post by Jamie Bonkiewicz is igniting intense debate online as Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth faces mounting calls for removal and formal impeachment proceedings on Capitol Hill.

Representative Thomas Massie has filed articles of impeachment against the Pentagon chief, with Article IV specifically citing the deadly February airstrike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls elementary school in Minab, Iran. The strike resulted in over 150 civilian casualties, predominantly young schoolchildren and teachers. While the Pentagon maintains that an internal command investigation remains underway and denies deliberately targeting civilians, lawmakers allege systematic breakdowns in civilian-protection protocols and target verification.

With pressure mounting from both sides of the aisle, do you think Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should resign, face impeachment, or remain in office?

Drop your thoughts below.

Staff Sergeant Workman was born on 26 August 1983 in Marion, Ohio. Prior to graduation from North Union High School in Richwood, Ohio, he enlisted in the Marine Corps on 28 August 2000 and reported for recruit training at Marine Corps Recruit Depot, Parris Island, South Carolina, on 19 August 2001 and graduated on 16 November 2001. Upon graduation, he reported to the School of Infantry at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, where he attained the MOS of 0341 (Mortarman).

In March of 2002, Private First Class Workman reported for duty at Marine Corps Security Forces Company in Kingsbay, Georgia. He was then assigned to 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines at Camp Pendleton, California, where he served in Weapons Company with the 81mm Mortar Platoon as a team leader and then as squad leader.

In September of 2004, Corporal Workman deployed to Iraq and participated in Operation Phantom Fury. On 23 December 2004, he led his squad in three separate intense fire fights during clearing operations in Al Fallujah, resulting in the rescue of injured Marines. His heroic actions contributed to the elimination of 24 insurgents, and he was awarded the Navy Cross.

Just across the border from El Paso, Texas, deported U.S. military veterans stood at attention in Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, saluting the American flag on Veterans Day.

Many enlisted as lawful permanent residents, served in Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan, and were later deported after criminal convictions or unprocessed citizenship paperwork. Advocates and groups like the Deported Veterans Support House ("Juárez Bunker") argue those who put their lives on the line in a U.S. uniform deserve a second chance and a path back home, while federal immigration law requires deportation for certain felony offenses even after military service.

Should non-citizen veterans who served honorably be protected from deportation, or should the same immigration laws apply?

A North Carolina high school student who was suspended for saying "illegal alien" during an English class has won a $20,000 settlement and a public apology from his school district (Carolina Journal).

Christian McGhee, then 16 years old at Central Davidson High School, received a three-day suspension in 2024 after asking his teacher whether a vocabulary word referred to "space aliens or illegal aliens who need green cards" (Liberty Justice Center).

Administrators labeled the remark racially insensitive, causing him to miss key track meets and prompting his family to file a federal First Amendment lawsuit with the Liberty Justice Center (Liberty Justice Center).

Under the federal court-approved agreement, the Davidson County Board of Education will pay $20,000, issue a formal public apology, and scrub any reference to racial bias from his school records (Carolina Journal).

Was this a major victory for student free speech, or should the school have handled it differently from day one?

"They're an evil enemy. They've killed many Americans," Trump said during the interview, as the White House continues navigating the fallout from the Iran conflict, rising energy tensions, and stalled diplomatic talks.

Supporters of stricter border enforcement argue that sovereign nations require clear rules, security vetting, and controlled entry to protect citizens and maintain order. Critics counter that faith-based analogies oversimplify complex humanitarian challenges and that immigration policy should prioritize compassion and legal pathways.

In 2013, Green Beret Nick Lavery was hit multiple times at point-blank range during an insider attack in Afghanistan, losing his leg above the knee after a grueling year of surgeries at Walter Reed.

Doctors expected him to medically retire. Nick chose combat instead.

Pushing through brutal physical evaluations, he became the first Special Forces operator in military history to return to combat as an above-the-knee amputee in 2015. He went on to conquer Special Forces Warrant Officer School, Combat Diver Qualification, and Special Operations Combatives Instructor training, earning the Silver Star and multiple Purple Hearts along the way.

What this man overcame redefines what humans are capable of.

Texas just put $17 an hour on the table.
For 17 years, Texas has been stuck at $7.25.
That’s not a living wage. That’s a survival wage. Now that Democrats control the Texas House, several bills were filed Monday to change that. One of them jumps the state minimum wage all the way to $17 an hour. Others land at $15.Republicans still control the Senate, so this is far from done. But the conversation just shifted hard. Some people will call it radical.
Others will call it the bare minimum after almost two decades of no raise while rent, groceries, and everything else kept climbing. Either way… the number is finally on the board.

Russia doubled its diesel exports to 271,000 barrels a day in October after President Donald Trump eased fuel sanctions and pressured Ukraine to pause refinery strikes, yet not a single shipment has reached the United States, according to the Financial Times.

Kpler data shows Russian cargoes surged to Brazil, Türkiye, and other buyers while at least two U.S.-bound tankers diverted and another (Agioi Fanendes) sat off the East Coast awaiting a buyer amid legal and state-level sanctions warnings. Meanwhile, U.S. diesel stockpiles dropped below 100 million barrels for the first time in over 20 years, and AAA's national diesel average sits at $6.10 a gallon.

Trump defended the Oct. 9 deal on Truth Social as "ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" to lower costs for Americans, while critics and Ukrainian leaders argued easing sanctions only helped Moscow recover. What do you make of this?

For the first time, the U.S. Marine Corps has spelled out exactly when a Marine can refuse a barracks room—and guaranteed they can't be punished for speaking up.

Under the updated Barracks "Bill of Rights," Marines can officially refuse quarters with mold, broken locks, no hot water, or unsafe walls and windows. Commanders are now required to brief every Marine on these protections, with the order stating that "compromises in habitability degrade warfighting capability and will not be tolerated under any circumstance."

Every old-school Marine is probably thinking about their worst squad bay right now. Do you think this actually changes things on base? Drop your thoughts below.

Retired Gunnery Sergeant JoAnna Mendoza (AZ-06) just broke the barrier after 20 years of service in the Navy and Marine Corps, including deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan and time as a drill instructor. This isn’t just a win for one Marine. It’s a record-setting wave of women who served our country now ready to serve in Congress.

The U.S. military has always been fertile soil for firsts throughout our nation’s history, and the promotion of Carol A. Mutter to become the nation’s first female lieutenant general serves as a perfect case in point for Women’s History Month.

Women have served in the military from the earliest years of our representative republic.

Deborah Sampson (Gannett) served covertly when she disguised herself as a man under the assumed name of Robert Shurtleff, to join the Continental Army and fight in the Revolutionary War in 1782. Sampson went so far as to cut a musket ball out of her own thigh to prevent a battlefield surgeon from discovering her true gender. She was honorably discharged as a private in 1793.

Women gained the opportunity to serve openly in World War 1 when Congress opened the military to women in 1914. However, it took more than two centuries between the time Sampson first shouldered a musket to the time when women served as general (flag rank) officers in the American military. Mutter achieved one-star brigadier general rank in 1991.

Three years later Mutter became the first woman in the history of America’s military to achieve two-star major general rank in 1994, and two years after that in 1996 she became the first woman to become a three-star lieutenant general in any American military branch.

Born in 1945 in Greeley, Colorado, Mutter graduated in 1967 from officer candidate school at the University of Northern Colorado as a second lieutenant in the Marine Corps.

Mutter had a number of firsts during her 32-year career in the Corps:

•First woman to qualify as Command Center Crew Commander/Space Director at U.S. Space Command.
• First woman of flag rank (general officer rank) to command a major deployable tactical command.
• First woman Marine major general, and senior woman in all the services at that time.
• First woman nominated by a U.S. president (Bill Clinton) for three-star rank.
• First female lieutenant general in the U.S. Armed Forces.

During a 2014 interview for the documentary Unsung Heroes: The Story of America's Female Patriots, Mutter explains why she joined the Marine Corps during the early years of the Vietnam War.

“Because they're the best, there's no doubt about that,” she said. “ ... when I joined, (the Corps) was only one percent female and there were no women in the deployed forces at all. So, as long as the women were back in the rear doing the jobs that the men didn't want to do, there was not much of a problem.”

The general has been recognized as a trailblazer by several different organizations. Among them is the National Women’s Hall of Fame, which inducted the general in 2017.

Mutter retired from the Corps in 1999 and lives with her husband at their home in Lookout Mountain, Tennessee.

On Sept. 8, 2009, during the Battle of Ganjgal in Kunar Province, Afghanistan, 21-year-old Marine Cpl. Dakota Meyer and Staff Sgt. Juan Rodriguez-Chavez heard their brothers trapped in a brutal ambush.

Denied permission four times to go in, Meyer defied orders, climbed into the gun turret of a Humvee, and charged into the kill zone five separate times across a six-hour firefight. Even after taking shrapnel to his arm, he helped rescue 36 Afghan and U.S. personnel and fought on foot to recover the bodies of his four fallen teammates — 1st Lt. Michael Johnson, Staff Sgt. Aaron Kenefick, Gunnery Sgt. Edwin Johnson, and Hospital Corpsman 3rd Class James Layton.

He was already on fire… and he still went back in.

Most people hear “Medal of Honor” and picture a single heroic moment.
This wasn’t one moment.On October 17, 2005, Sgt. 1st Class Alwyn C. Cashe’s Bradley was hit by an IED in Iraq and turned into an inferno. Fuel soaked him. His uniform caught fire.He still pulled the driver out.
Then he went back.
And back again.
And again. Six of his soldiers. While he was burning. He refused to be evacuated until every one of them was out first. He died three weeks later from the burns covering most of his body. Sixteen years later, they finally upgraded his Silver Star to the Medal of Honor. Some men talk about never leaving a brother behind.
Cashe lived it while he was on fire.

Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed is going straight after Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., calling him a "profound failure" and vowing Senate probes after Democrats' 2026 midterm victories.

El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former Michigan health official, previously accused Kennedy of gutting public health protections while still failing to deliver on food and pharma promises. Meanwhile, Kennedy pushed back at a MAHA Action event, arguing nothing is going to get in his way now as incoming House and Senate Democrats prepare major oversight investigations.

Where do you stand on RFK Jr.'s job as HHS Secretary so far? Drop your take below.

SSG Jamyn Peterson wouldn't describe himself as a hero, he said. However, during his last deployment to the remote Oruzgan province in Afghanistan from December 2006 until January 2008, the Army Reservist repeatedly demonstrated his dedication to his comrades and to his duties. Peterson was recognized for his service with a Purple Heart and two Bronze Star Medals, one with ‘Valor.'

The second Bronze Star recognized his performance as team leader as “absolutely phenomenal,” according to the award citation. But it was the bravery he demonstrated during an ambush that earned him the Bronze Star with ‘Valor.”

“I was honored,” Peterson said of receiving the medal, “but I was more honored that my guys got them.”

SSG Matt Winters and SGT Ben Mogenson were riding with him on June 16, 2007 when their convoy was ambushed on the road home. When a bomb exploded just feet from their truck, the truck leading the convoy sped ahead to avoid the blast. But they took a wrong turn.

Peterson and his team had a choice: stay on the road that led back to camp or follow their comrades the wrong way into enemy territory. They decided to follow their comrades.

It wasn't long before the first truck was hit by a rocket propelled grenade that went right through it, forcing everyone out of the truck. And while there were
only six soldiers between their two trucks, “there were over 100 bad guys. They were only 90 feet away. You could see them. They were just lined up,” he said.
“It was like hail coming down on the truck. It was like incessant bullets raining,” Peterson said. That's when he directed his vehicle right into the middle of the ambush to provide cover and support to the disabled vehicle.

“The one thing I remember was that I could have stayed in the truck and gotten killed, but if I got out of the truck I was going to get killed. Pretty much we were going to die,” he said. “Life flashes before you.”

But Peterson did get out of the truck, and was able to set up behind the hood of the disabled vehicle so he could provide cover while the other soldiers tended to the injured. They were able to hold the enemy at bay until Afghan Army soldiers arrived on the scene to help. When the enemy saw the two trucks with 15 Afghan soldiers in it, they started to flee, Peterson said.

“They kind of saved our lives,” Peterson said. “We'd built enough of a rapport,” he said, “that they came to help us.” It was an act which demonstrated not only their loyalty, but also their bravery, he said.

Peterson spoke as highly of Winters and Mogenson.

“They were more aware of what was going on. That's more brave than me,” he said. “Those guys were aware what was going on and still kept at it. They did a great job.”

Peterson, however, said he is most proud of his work with the people of the Oruzgan province. Working with the local community, he and his team set up the only local health clinic for miles around, a radio station, as well as a primary school for the local children that teaches reading, writing, arithmetic and Islam.

“Any good we wanted to do, we were able to do it,” Peterson said. “Being out in the middle of nowhere, I thought I was in a place where I belonged.”

Despite the enemy's opposition to the school, the students would get up at five in the morning to walk five miles to school. They would have to skirt Taliban checkpoints to avoid getting beaten, Peterson said.

“They are worried if they're going to get beaten with sticks on the way to school, and they'd still come,” Peterson said. The enemy “rocketed us twice while the students were in there, but they kept coming.”

“It was a pretty amazing experience. A good learning experience,” he said of the deployment. “That's one thing that I take away from this, how the human being can adapt to any situation.”

Peterson is still an active reservist training troops heading to Afghanistan.

“That's what I have a passion for now, making sure that these troops are ready to hit the ground when they go down range,” he said.

Peterson, who will likely redeploy shortly, said it's important to remember that the army is made up of individual men and women.

“If I don't go, someone less experienced will have to go. There's an obligation there,” he said. “Somebody's got to do it.”

Federal prosecutors have indicted a former bodyguard for Rep. Ilhan Omar on a felony charge of lying under oath in immigration paperwork amid a broader immigration fraud probe, according to reports.

Omar's office pushed back against the indictment, calling it political retaliation and accusing federal investigators of pressuring the former security guard for information—while prosecutors move forward with the case.

What's your take on how this investigation is unfolding? Drop your thoughts below.

One day after an Army sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier called out Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his aides for laughing during a Veterans Day visit, Hegseth welcomed the soldier to the Pentagon and pinned the Joint Service Commendation Medal on his uniform.

Specialist Iglesias of the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment—The Old Guard—had stopped his patrol on November 11 to remind the group that "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times." Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the soldier acted "correctly and respectfully," and Hegseth praised him for upholding standards.

Respecting the Tomb isn't optional, no matter who you are. What's your take on how both sides handled this?

Sergeant Matthew Abbate sprinted around in a live minefield, breaking an enemy ambush, clearing a landing zone, and evacuating critically wounded casualties.

Sgt Abbate, a Scout Sniper from 3rd Battalion, 5th Marines, patrolled with his squad through Sangin, Afghanistan on October 14, 2010. Taliban fighters opened up on the Marines from multiple positions. The patrol leader fell. The rest of the squad scattered for cover. As they spread out, two Marines and the patrol Corpsman suddenly stepped on anti-personnel mines, knocking them down one by one in rapid succession. The Marines were unaware they had entered a live minefield. Still under fire, Abbate ignored the danger and sprinted through the area, directing the remaining Marines onto targets and suppressing the enemy with his own weapon. The Taliban broke contact in the face of the Marines' accurate fire.

Abbate called for emergency medevac for the wounded, then swept the area for remaining explosives that could prevent a chopper from landing. While he cleared the LZ, the Taliban resumed their attack. MARINE CORPS AIR GROUND COMBAT CENTER TWENTYNINE PALMS, Calif. --

Famous French emperor Napoleon Bonaparte once said, “Valor is a gift. Those having it never know for sure whether they have it till the test comes.”
In a ceremony at Lance Cpl. Torrey L. Gray Field Thursday, a Marine who was tested in the heat of battle received the highest award for valor given by the Department of the Navy, the Navy Cross Medal, and was meritoriously promoted to the rank of corporal.

Cpl. Richard S. Weinmaster, a Squad Automatic Weapon gunner with 3rd Platoon, Company E, 2nd Battalion, 7th Marine Regiment, received the award for his actions as a private first class in Afghanistan’s Helmand Province on July 8, 2008 in support of Operation Enduring Freedom.

According to his platoon commander, 1st Lt. George Fenton, Weinmaster, a Cozad, Neb., native, was in front of a squad-sized patrol making its way through an eight-foot wide alley bordered on each side by 10-foot tall mud-brick walls, dubbed “ambush alley,” when their patrol was attacked by enemy small-arms fire and grenades.

In the midst of the firefight, Weinmaster provided accurate suppressive fire with his SAW until he noticed an incoming grenade land near his team leader, Lance Cpl. Tyler Wilkerson.

Fenton, a Fredericksburg, Va., native, explained how Weinmaster shoved Wilkerson out of the way then jumped toward the grenade to try and smother the blast. As he jumped, the grenade exploded sending the majority of its shrapnel into Weinmaster.

Weinmaster effectively shielded his team leader from the blast and Wilkerson was spared from any shrapnel. Weinmaster, however, received serious wounds, including a piece of shrapnel that entered his left eye socket and traveled halfway into his brain, where it remains to this day.

Despite his grave injuries, Weinmaster re-mounted his SAW and continued to provide effective suppressive fire on the enemy positions 50 yards away.

Staff Sgt. Kyle Lockhart, Weinmaster’s former platoon sergeant, said Weinmaster’s heroic actions in the heat of battle are a true reflection of his caliber.

Lockhart said for a Marine two-and-a-half months into his first deployment who has been in the Marine Corps for just a year to show such heroism is proof real valor and selflessness remain in the heart of Marines everywhere.

“Valor has to come from the heart and soul,” said Jim Weinmaster, Cpl. Weinmaster’s father. “It has to come from within. Karen [Weinmaster’s mother] and I raised him as best as we could, but actions like that go beyond parenting, beyond anything that can be taught.”

Weinmaster remained humble throughout the ceremony as well as afterward when he was greeted and thanked by scores of Marines, former Marines and grateful civilians.

“I didn’t do anything special,” he told everyone. “Everyone on my left and right would have done the same thing. I was just in the right place at the right time.”

Fenton and Lockhart agreed, saying that their platoon was full of Marines who would have done the same if given the opportunity, but both also emphasized the fact Weinmaster was given the opportunity and he acted in total disregard for his own safety to save another Marine’s life.

His devotion and selflessness earned Weinmaster the Navy Cross, although he maintains he was “just doing his job.”

Mike Morton's path is one of the most remarkable stories in military and endurance sports history.

Named Ultrarunner of the Year and inducted into the American Ultrarunning Hall of Fame in 2024, Mike Morton proved that some men simply refuse to quit.

Ivan M. Ruiz, Air Force Cross Recipient
Home of record: Galloway, New Jersey

Awarded for actions during the Global War on Terror

The President of the United States of America, authorized by section 8742 of Title 10 U.S.C., takes pleasure in presenting the Air Force Cross to Master Sergeant Ivan M. Ruiz for extraordinary heroism in military operations against an armed enemy of the United States as a Pararescue Craftsman, 22 Expeditionary Special Tactics Squadron, Combined Joint Special Operations Air Component-Afghanistan, in Kandahar Province, Afghanistan, on 10 December 2013. On that date, Sergeant Ruiz attached to a team of Army Special Forces personnel and Afghan Commandos conducting a raid in denied terrain. After a point blank engagement with four insurgents, Sergeant Ruiz's team continued to clear a small compound of resistance while maneuvering towards neutralized insurgents to search their remains. Isolated from the 14 man element, Sergeant Ruiz and two teammates encountered a vicious insurgent crossfire, sweeping the courtyard with small arms fire and throwing hand grenades from barricaded strongpoints. Sergeant Ruiz eliminated one enemy fighter with well-aimed carbine fire, while enemy fire wounded his two comrades, rendering them immobile and exposed to enemy fire. Alone in the courtyard, Sergeant Ruiz completely disregarded his personal safety and refused to withdraw to cover. Single-handedly suppressing enemy fire until reinforcements arrived, Sergeant Ruiz pressed ahead under intense fire to reach his wounded comrades. Drawing fire from the enemy and returning fire to prevent the insurgents from maneuvering, he was gradually driven into a prone fighting position by the sheer volume of enemy fire. His refusal to leave the courtyard prevented enemy fighters from engaging his wounded teammates with direct fire weapons, though enemy grenades impacted within five meters of Sergeant Ruiz's position. Eventually joined by teammates, Sergeant Ruiz advanced through a hail of machine gun fire and grenades to drag a wounded teammate back to a position of relative cover and concealment. While still dangerously exposed to gunfire raking the compound, Sergeant Ruiz administered life-saving trauma care to his teammates while wearing night vision goggles. Sergeant Ruiz's heroic actions through intense enemy fire saved the lives of two teammates and contributed to eleven insurgents killed. Through his extraordinary heroism, superb airmanship, and aggressiveness in the face of the enemy, Sergeant Ruiz reflected the highest credit upon himself and the United States Air Force.

FORT BRAGG, N.C. -- Thomas Barbieri loves it when people ask about the World War II replica motorcycle he built because it lets him talk about his son, T.J.

Barbieri and his sons Stephen, Matt, and David painstakingly assembled the bike over nine months as a way to pay tribute to the second oldest Barbieri boy, T.J., who was killed in Iraq in August 2006 at the age of 24.

"When you lose someone, you always want to tell their story," Barbieri said. "When people see the bike, they start asking questions, and I get to tell them about T.J."

His father said that from an early age, Thomas J. "T.J." Barbieri was always interested in military history. That interest eventually led him to enlist in the Army and become a Paratrooper in the 82nd Airborne Division. At the time of his death, he was a Specialist with the 1st Battalion, 325th Airborne Infantry Regiment, 2nd Brigade Combat Team.

He loved being a Soldier, said his father. "He considered (his unit) a second family," Thomas Barbieri said.
T.J. was awarded the Silver Star for his actions during the engagement that cost him his life. According to the citation, he exposed himself in full view of the enemy in order to rescue his platoon sergeant and others trapped in the kill zone of an ambush. T.J. killed one enemy fighter and was still shooting his weapon even as he was struck down by enemy fire.

"He always talked about being a hero, and that's what he was," said his mother, Carolann Barbieri. "That's how he died, a hero."

Since T.J.'s death, his family has stayed in touch with members of his unit and become increasingly involved in programs that help wounded veterans at Walter Reed Army Medical Center, not far from the family home in Gaithersburg, Md.

Eventually, the Barbieris decided they wanted to do something as a family that would be a lasting testament to T.J. Given T.J.'s lifelong interest in the military and WWII history, they decided that recreating a WWII Army motorcycle would be a fitting tribute.

"We thought it would be a nice family project to build it in tribute to him," Thomas Barbieri said.

To replicate the WWII-era Harley Davidson WLA bike, Thomas Barbieri and his three sons stripped down a modern Harley. They modified some parts of the bike and replicated others to give it the look of a motorcycle from 65 years ago.

"We tried to recreate a bike as close as possible to what a WLA bike actually looked like," Barbieri said.

When it was done, the Barbieris unveiled it for the first time for some of the Soldiers at Walter Reed. "The response was really cool," Barbieri said. "The Soldiers seemed to love it." The Barbieri family of Gaithersburg, Md., built this replica of a World War II era Harley Davidson WLA motorcycle in honor of Spc. Thomas "T.J." Barbieri, a paratrooper with the 82nd Airborne Division's 2nd Brigade Combat Team, was killed in Iraq in 2006.

The Barbieri family of Gaithersburg, Md., built this replica of a World War II era Harley Davidson WLA motorcycle in honor of Spc. Thomas "T.J." Barbieri, a paratrooper with the 82nd Airborne Division's 2nd Brigade Combat Team, was killed in Iraq in 2006.

For the Barbieris, the bike was a labor of love, and they have been compensated beyond measure for the time and effort that went into it.

"There was a tremendous sense of gratification that we were doing something in remembrance of him," Thomas Barbieri said.

On patrol in al Bawi, Iraq, First Lieutenant Ross Pixler was in the lead inside his armored Bradley Fighting Vehicle on an October day when the fiery blast of an IED shattered the daily monotony. The deeply buried IED exploded as the Bradley passed over, ripping the vehicle apart and killing three fellow soldiers.

Still dazed by the carnage, Pixler exemplified the strength of an army soldier by ignoring his injuries, finding his rifle, and getting to work. Already, the three other vehicles in the convoy were approaching the attack site, but Pixler wasted no time in checking on the unconscious driver and gunner and taking up a defensive position. He later reflected, “Everything goes really fast, and I wasn't really stopping to think about what I was doing. I was doing what I was trained to do.”

Just as Pixler and the rest of his unit began recovering from the attack, scattered mortar and small arms fire bombarded the site. Pixler, rattled by his concussion, did not hesitate to raise his rifle and take a key role in the defense of the position while assistance came to recover the bodies of the Americans.

As the hours wore on, Pixler and the other surviving members of his team were loaded onto another Bradley and pulled out of the waning firefight. The safety of the rescue vehicle was broken when another IED crippled it, forcing the men to exit the vehicle and repulse another attack.

It took many hours from the initial attack to get Pixler and his men inside the walls of an American base, but his focus on the mission and his men never wavered.

For his bravery under such austere conditions and his tenacity in the face of adversity, he earned the prestigious Silver Star medal. Pixler considers it not an award for himself but “an award for every single one of the soldiers that were out there, and the ones that can't come home.”

In the military you adapt to the mission and the hours. For Army MAJ Robert Nesbit Jr., that meant performing about 99% of his missions at night. He was deployed to Iraq from June 2006 to September 2007, as a troop commander.

"Over the course of the tour there were more than a few tough nights,” said Nesbit. "But there was one single night that stands out.” That incident led to him being awarded both an Army Commendation Medal with Valor device and a Purple Heart. It also was part of the reason he received the Bronze Star.

In October 2006, Nesbit was stationed in Baghdad with the 1-14th Cavalry. His squadron was in a neighborhood known as Abu-Dichir, and his mission was to "create a ‘safe neighborhood' in the squadron's battle space.”

"At the time there was a lot of violence directed by the insurgents against the local population and we were trying to protect them,” explained Nesbit.

One of the things Nesbit and his team of about 80 soldiers did was place concrete barricades across streets to prevent vehicle access.

"Emplacing concrete barriers always attracted a lot of attention which was part of why we normally operated at night,” he continued.
"On Oct. 22, 2006, we [the Troop Team Task Force] were en-route to start our mission for the night when the Stryker I was on was blown up in an ambush. There were four of us on board who were wounded, said Nesbit.

"Long story short, I got the other three soldiers medivaced off of the battlefield. Even though I was hurt, I chose to stay in the fight. Not for any sense of heroics, but rather, I felt as the commander as long as I physically could still move the soldiers deserved for me to stay and command,” Nesbit continued.

"A lot went into it, and it was a long night, but we got the ambush defeated,” he said.

All of the unit's equipment was recovered, and they were able to return to their Forward Operating Base.

"The next night I was back out leading the mission. I was awarded the Purple Heart for being wounded that night, and I was awarded the ARCOM w/V for continuing to fight while wounded,” he stated. "There were other nights and other fights, but that one certainly stands out for me personally,” Nesbit concluded.

He received the Bronze Star for his service, work ethic and leadership as the troop commander during this deployment.
